title: Accessible Content and Visuals

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Accessible Content and Visuals.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Accessible content is not a duplicate textual layer attached after visual design. It is information designed so its purpose and relationships remain perceivable and understandable through varied senses, technologies, languages, and conditions.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at preserve purpose, structure, and consequence?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use semantic structure—page title, landmarks, headings, lists, tables, labels, instructions, and relationships—rather than relying on size and position. Reading order should follow task meaning when CSS and spatial layout are removed. Link text should identify destination or purpose in context.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Do not use colour as the only cue. Combine it with visible text, shape, pattern, icon, or position, and ensure those alternatives are also programmatically available. Contrast supports perception, but passing a contrast ratio cannot rescue tiny type, dense layout, glare, poor hierarchy, or confusing content.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Text alternatives depend on purpose:

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: decorative images usually need to be ignored by assistive technology; functional images need an accessible name describing the action; informative images need the information they uniquely convey; complex diagrams may need a concise alternative plus structured detail, data table, or adjacent explanation.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: “Image of chart” inventories an object but does not communicate its conclusion. Repeating a visible caption creates noise.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at design meaning across transformations?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Run transformation checks:

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: remove colour—do statuses and selection survive? remove images—does essential instruction remain? remove sound—are speech and alerts captioned or otherwise available? remove spatial layout—does source and reading order still make sense? enlarge text and reflow—do relationships and actions remain usable? pause motion—does information persist and control remain?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: translate—do labels, lengths, grammar, and cultural assumptions hold? simplify language—are material details preserved rather than omitted?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Plain language reduces unnecessary cognitive demand: familiar words, concrete verbs, informative headings, short purposeful sentences, and explanations near decisions. It does not mean childish tone or removal of medical consequence. Define essential specialist terms and layer detail so people can inspect it.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: financial chart?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A red line falling below a green line may indicate loss visually. Accessible presentation names series, labels important values, explains the period and conclusion, provides underlying data, and avoids assuming that “up” is always good. Alternative text should convey the decision-relevant relationship, not every pixel.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at where this can go wrong?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Colour-only state: hue carries success, error, or selection. Pixel-inventory alternative: appearance is described without information or purpose. Visual-order dependence: non-visual reading separates labels, values, and actions. Plain-language deletion: brevity removes risks or conditions needed for informed choice.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Placeholder accessibility: sample copy passes while real data and translation break layout. Separate accessible version: a neglected alternative receives different content or outcome.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Preserve meaning across sensory and language conditions
turns.text: What changes when we look at preserve meaning across sensory and language conditions?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Readable content uses clear structure, descriptive headings, meaningful link text, plain language appropriate to the audience, and explanations for necessary clinical terms. Text must survive zoom, reflow, custom spacing, translation, and high contrast. Instructions do not depend on “the green button on the right,” and error identification is specific enough to recover.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Accessible content needs governance. Build required fields, status semantics, alternatives, heading rules, contrast tokens, reflow behaviour, and translation tolerance into the content model and design system. Editorial workflows should prevent publication when essential alternatives are absent. Procurement must cover third-party charts, media, and documents.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Test content changes as product changes.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Preserve meaning beyond one visual treatment
turns.text: What changes when we look at preserve meaning beyond one visual treatment?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Visual simplification cannot remove uncertainty or clinical distinction. Text alternatives depend on purpose; decorative images are ignored, informative diagrams have equivalent explanation, and charts expose underlying values. Content is tested at 400% zoom, high contrast, translated length, screen-reader navigation, and custom text spacing.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: <! -- Editorial: manual revision; curated product example --

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Illustrative scenario: a weather alert. A red warning card is prominent to some readers but ambiguous to others and silent to a screen reader if the status is only visual. Pair colour with words and structure; make the warning readable at zoom; ensure it is announced at the right time.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Test whether people understand the risk and next action, not merely whether the palette passes a contrast checker.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Find one interface where status depends on colour, position, or icon. Describe the meaning aloud without referencing appearance. If that is difficult, the information model—not only the styling—needs work.
